claims.text: LLM-generated summaries of scientific abstracts are twice as likely to contain generalized conclusions compared to the original abstracts.
Newer LLM models overgeneralized scientific conclusions in 26% to 73% of tested cases.
LLM-generated article summaries were nearly five times more likely to contain broad generalizations than human-authored NEJM Journal Watch summaries.
Generating summaries at an LLM temperature setting of 0 reduces the likelihood of generalized conclusions by 76% compared to a temperature of 0.7.
Prompts explicitly instructing LLMs to avoid inaccuracies roughly doubled the likelihood of generating overgeneralized conclusions compared to simple prompts.
Claude models (Claude 2, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and Claude 3.7 Sonnet) did not produce a statistically significant increase in generalized conclusions compared to original scientific texts.

evidence.description: GLMM regression showed all combined LLM summaries were significantly more likely to contain generalized conclusions than original scientific abstracts (B = 0.693, SE = 0.1926, p < 0.001).
DeepSeek, ChatGPT-4o, and LLaMA 3.3 70B exhibited overall algorithmic overgeneralization rates ranging between 26% and 73% across different prompts on scientific abstracts.
In direct comparison to NEJM Journal Watch summaries of 100 medical articles, LLM summaries had an odds ratio of 4.85 (95% CI [3.06, 7.70], p < 0.001) for containing generalized conclusions.
GLMM temperature comparison demonstrated that temperature 0.0 vs temperature 0.7 yielded B = -1.432 (SE = 0.3726, p < 0.001), indicating a 76% lower likelihood of generalized conclusions.
GLMM regression showed the accuracy prompt increased the likelihood of generalized conclusions compared to the simple prompt with an odds ratio of 1.90 (95% CI [1.11, 3.26], p = 0.020).
Statistical comparison against original abstracts yielded p = 0.685 for Claude 2, p = 0.587 for Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and p = 0.064 for Claude 3.7 Sonnet.

methodologies.name: LLM generalization benchmarking framework
methodologies.description: A comparative content-analysis framework evaluating scientific summaries by coding result claims into generic, present-tense, or action-guiding generalizations and analyzing scope transitions using generalized linear mixed models.
datasets: 200 scientific abstracts (100 general medical, 100 multidisciplinary science)
100 NEJM Journal Watch expert human summaries
conditions: 10 LLM models (GPT-3.5 Turbo, GPT-4 Turbo, ChatGPT-4o, ChatGPT-4.5, LLaMA 2 70B, LLaMA 3.3 70B, Claude 2, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, DeepSeek)

limitations.text: The study evaluated only three specific prompt variations.

Full-length article summary comparisons were limited to a subset of models (GPT-4 Turbo, ChatGPT-4o, DeepSeek) evaluated against a single expert human source (NEJM Journal Watch), which may not reflect all human science communicators.
The evaluation focused predominantly on medical and general multidisciplinary science texts, so results may not generalize to other specific scientific disciplines.
Prior research had not systematically examined whether LLMs accurately preserve the generalization scope of scientific research.

future_work.text: Examine how LLM overgeneralization tendencies differ across diverse scientific text domains such as foundational versus applied research.
Investigate prompt transformation ('shadow prompting') to enforce past-tense summarization of scientific results as a mitigation strategy.
Test LLMs instructed to adopt specific user personas, such as university press officers or marketing writers, to determine variation in overgeneralization rates.
